splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the end of the prior plan year, allowing the use of updated information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms are not tolled by absconding, meaning the court's authority expires at the end of the original term regardless of the supervisee's flight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h) for successive collateral attacks. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners, who need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects whether election administration challenges must wait until after elections, when they may become moot or create chaos, or whether candidates have automatic or near-automatic standing to challenge rules before an election.

positions.label: Standing exists for candidates
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules before an election takes place, recognizing a cognizable competitive injury from allegedly unlawful voting procedures.

positions.label: Standing does not exist for candidates
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election absent a more particularized showing of injury, denying that generalized competitive harm suffices.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps judicial deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal statutes and sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity should prevail over deference (whether Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary or Chevron deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions. This split has deepened after the Supreme Court overruled Chevron in Loper Bright and narrowed Auer deference in Kisor.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt within 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects career-offender designations and sentence lengths for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative, binding interpretation of the career-offender guideline and properly includes conspiracy, attempt, and aiding and abetting within 'controlled substance offense.'

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to the definition rather than interpreting it, and thus is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one of the criteria is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for many federal drug defendants and creates geographic sentencing disparities.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can support compassionate release and whether the Sentencing Commission can authorize courts to consider such changes. This affects many federal prisoners serving long sentences under laws Congress later amended but did not make retroactive.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction, and the Sentencing Commission's attempt to say otherwise exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the nature of the violation and the need to deter future violations.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may be based on punishment, with the Sixth Circuit allowing district courts to expressly impose punitive revocation sentences while other circuits prohibit punishment as a justification. This affects hundreds of individuals facing revocations annually.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible basis for revocation sentences
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, allowing punitive considerations in revocation sentencing.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible basis for revocation sentences
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release is not a punishment for the violation itself, and sentencing upon revocation must focus on the defendant's breach of trust and the need to deter future violations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses state drug offenses involving substances not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' reference to 'an offense under state law' requires that the substance be controlled under federal law. This affects career-offender and other guideline calculations for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances scheduled differently under state and federal law.

positions.label: State offenses qualify regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b)'s broad reference to 'an offense under state law' includes offenses involving substances controlled only under state law, even if not federally scheduled.

positions.label: State offenses must involve federally controlled substances
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if it involves a substance that is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may bring civil rights claims, and whether challenges to BOP decisions regarding First Step Act earned time credits are cognizable in habeas.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement, or whether civil rights actions are also available. This split has become newly relevant in the context of First Step Act earned time credit disputes over expedited transfer to prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions/terms challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available to challenge BOP decisions about conditions or terms of confinement, including First Step Act time credit determinations regarding prerelease custody.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and challenges to conditions or terms must be brought through civil rights actions like Bivens.

circuits.name: Tenth Circuit
circuits.caseName: McIntosh v. United States Parole Commission

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceedings, so the shorter criminal appeal deadline governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable as collateral orders because the privacy interest in medical information is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost if review were delayed. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of collateral orders, creating potential disagreement about the scope of the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Immediately appealable as collateral order
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records meet the collateral order doctrine requirements because medical privacy is a value of high order that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders, including those involving medical information, are not immediately appealable collateral orders because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment or through other means.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtors upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This affects debtors' ability to retain equity gains in their homes during lengthy Chapter 13 cases that ultimately convert to Chapter 7 liquidation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors, as § 348(f)(1)(A) was enacted to protect good-faith converting debtors from losing value accumulated during their Chapter 13 plan.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted cert to resolve disagreements about the legal standards for discrimination claims in business or hospitality settings. The grant indicates the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied legal standards for discrimination in hospitality settings that the Supreme Court found sufficiently questionable to grant certiorari for review.

positions.label: Conflicting approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business or hospitality establishments, creating the disagreement that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's claim seeking expedited transfer to prerelease custody based on earned time credits under the First Step Act must be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may also be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: Circuits have long disagreed on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) are cognizable only in habeas or may also be brought under civil rights statutes. This split has been applied to First Step Act time-credit disputes, with circuits differing on whether such claims fall under habeas or Bivens/§ 1983.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that claims seeking speedier release from imprisonment, including FSA time-credit claims for expedited transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought as habeas petitions under § 2241.

positions.label: Civil rights claims may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or BOP program decisions may be brought through civil rights actions and are not exclusively cognizable in habeas, particularly when the relief sought does not necessarily shorten the sentence.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
